title: Sex-specific differences in running injuries: a systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression
authors: Hollander K, Rahlf AL, Wilke J, Edler C, Steib S, Junge A, Zech A
population: 38 prospective studies of running-related injury rates in both sexes (31 pooled)
findings: Overall injury rate was 20.8 (95% CI 19.9-21.7) per 100 female runners vs 20.4 (95% CI 19.7-21.1) per 100 male runners.
No sex difference for overall injuries per 100 runners (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.90-1.10, n = 24) or per hour/athlete exposure (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.69-1.27, n = 6).
Bone stress injury was more frequent in females (RR for males 0.52, 95% CI 0.36-0.76, n = 5); Achilles tendinopathy more frequent in males (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.25-2.79, n = 2).
Meta-regression: higher injury risk in female runners with competition distances of 10 km and shorter (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.00-1.69, as printed in the abstract).
limitations: Subgroup pools are small (2-6 studies); heterogeneous injury definitions; no information about load progression.
implications: Do not apply a sex-based difference to overall load-progression caps.
Sex should only modulate injury-specific cautions (female: bone-stress vigilance; male: Achilles tendon vigilance), not volume limits.

verification.notes: Crossref: Sports Med 51:1011-1039 (online Jan 2021). Abstract matched. The printed meta-regression CI (1.00-1.69 around 1.08) looks asymmetric and is flagged as printed.
